check:0:0.q: Why not “To bill the team for the tokens its trial alrea…”?
check:0:0.a:
That option is tempting because tokens and money are linked. Every token costs something, and the trial did use tokens. So it is right that tokens matter for spending.

But it misses what the question asks for. "Tokens a minute at its busiest" is a **peak**. It is the highest rate in any single minute, not a total. A bill is about the total used over the whole trial. One busy minute tells you almost nothing about that total.

It also looks backward. The trial already ran inside the shared experiment space, under its own spending limit. Nobody needs this number to charge for the past.

Cost already has its own place in the pack: `cost_per_success`. That covers the money side.

The `peak_tpm` number looks forward. A **rate limit** is a cap on how many tokens a minute the deployment will accept. The platform team uses `peak_tpm` to set that cap on the new production capacity. If the cap is lower than the app's busiest minute, calls get refused.

"To size the capacity it moves to so it is not rate limited on day one" is better because it uses the peak for its real job: making sure the new home can handle the app's busiest minute from the start.

check:0:1.q: Why not “To check that its answers are right before real…”?
check:0:1.a:
Checking that answers are right before real users see them is a real goal. The graduation pack covers it, just with other evidence. The eval pass rate and the must-pass questions show whether the answers are good.

`peak_tpm` measures something different. It counts how many tokens (the small chunks of text a model reads and writes) the app sends through the model in its busiest minute. That number says nothing about whether an answer is correct. A wrong answer and a right answer can use the same tokens.

What the number does tell you is how much traffic to plan for. In the shared experiment space, each person has a rate limit, which is a cap on how many tokens a minute they may use. Production capacity also has a limit, and the platform team sets it for the app. If they set it below the app's busiest minute, calls get turned away on the first busy morning.

"To size the capacity it moves to so it is not rate limited on day one" is better because sizing capacity is exactly what the busiest-minute token count is for.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Pass: the numbers are good”?
check:1:0.a:
"Pass: the numbers are good" gets one thing right. The pass rate, the must-pass questions and the cost per success all meet their limits. Those checks really do pass.

But the gate checks six things, not just the numbers. Two of them are about who looks after the app and how they find out it's broken.

- **Owner**: a named person who fixes things. Without one, a problem lands on nobody's desk. That is one of the reasons the app is leaving the shared experiment space.
- **Monitoring**: alerts that tell the owner when the app breaks. Without them, failures stay quiet. Users notice before anyone on the team does.

Good numbers say the app works today. Owner and monitoring say someone will catch it when it stops working. Skipping them is graduating on enthusiasm, just with better charts.

Also, the gate never stops at "mostly fine." It keeps every failure it finds.

"Two problems: no owner, no monitoring" is better because it reports every check that fails, so the team can fix both in one round.

judge.notes: No real problems. The line 'Users notice before anyone on the team does' goes slightly beyond the lesson's 'quiet failures' but does not contradict it.

check:1:2.q: Why not “One problem: the first it finds”?
check:1:2.a:
"One problem: the first it finds" gets one thing right. The pack really does fail. No owner means the app can't graduate, so a gate that stops there still blocks it.

What it misses is how this gate is built. It doesn't stop at the first failed check. It walks through all six rules, one after another. Each rule that fails adds its reason to a list, and the gate keeps going to the end.

Picture the "first problem only" version. It reports "no owner." The team names an owner and sends the pack back. Only then does the gate say "no monitoring" (no alerts to tell the owner when the app breaks). That's a second round of waiting for a problem that was already there the first time.

The lesson's goal is to list every failure at once, so the team can fix them all in one round.

"Two problems: no owner, no monitoring" is better because it matches what the gate actually does: it checks every rule and reports every failure together, so nothing is hidden for a later round.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Its answers slowly get less accurate”?
check:2:0.a:
"Its answers slowly get less accurate" describes a real worry. Apps can drift. The questions people ask change, or the data behind the app goes stale. Evals and monitoring are how you catch that.

But that problem isn't caused by the shared experiment space. A slow slide in accuracy could happen just as easily on production capacity. Moving the app wouldn't fix it.

The question asks what could go wrong because of *where* the app runs. In the shared space, everyone uses one model deployment. A deployment here means one running copy of the model that handles requests. That copy can only handle so many tokens a minute. If someone's busy experiment uses up that capacity, your popular app gets rate-limited. Rate-limited means its requests are turned away or delayed. Users see failures, and nobody is named as the owner to fix it.

"A busy experiment eats its capacity" is better because it names the risk that comes from sharing one deployment, which is exactly what graduation removes.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Its eval scores reset every week”?
check:2:1.a:
"Its eval scores reset every week" sounds plausible, but nothing in the lesson says that happens. It isn't a real risk of the shared experiment space.

An **eval score** is the pass rate from running the app against a set of test questions. Those results are evidence the POC (the small trial build) measured. The team keeps them in the graduation pack, for example as metrics on an MLflow run. Where the app runs does not wipe them.

What the option gets right: it is worried about losing track of quality. That is a fair instinct. It just blames the wrong thing.

What it misses is the real danger. The shared space has **one model deployment for everyone**. Each person gets a spending limit and a rate limit (a cap on how many tokens they can use a minute). But they all draw from the same pool. A popular app sitting there competes with everyone's trials. Also, nobody is named to fix it when it breaks.

"A busy experiment eats its capacity" is better because it names the actual problem: shared capacity means someone else's heavy trial can starve an app people rely on.

judge.notes: No significant problems; the claim that where the app runs does not wipe eval scores is an inference the lesson does not state, and the answer is close to the 200-word limit.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Check every rule, keep every failure” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

*The problem:* "Before an app leaves the shared experiment space, a gate checks its evidence against limits we agreed on up front. If the gate stops at the first failure, the team fixes one thing, reruns, and hits the next failure. That wastes rounds."

*The idea:* "So the gate checks every rule and keeps every failure. Each failed rule adds a plain reason to a list. An empty list means the app graduates. Otherwise the team gets the full to-do list at once. The platform team also sizes capacity from the same numbers."

*The edge case:* "Boundaries must be explicit. I treat a value exactly at the limit as passing, and I write that down with the criteria before the trial starts. Then nobody argues about it later."

**A follow-up an interviewer might ask**

"Why write the acceptance criteria before the proof of concept, not after?"

*Hint for a strong answer:* If you set limits after seeing results, it is tempting to bend them so the app passes. Fixing them first keeps the gate honest. It also tells the trial what to measure, such as the cost per success and the tokens a minute at peak.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs after launch**

- **Rate-limit errors in the first week.** Calls get rejected with "too many requests" (HTTP 429) at busy times. Capacity was guessed, not sized from a measured peak.
- **A surprise bill.** Spend per day is far above what the trial suggested. Often the cost per success was worked out from passing runs only, which hides the cost of the failed ones.
- **Quiet failures.** Users complain before any alert fires, and nobody knows who should fix it. That means no named owner and no monitoring.
- **Answers that seemed fine in the trial now go wrong in real use.** The eval score looked good, but must-pass questions were never checked one by one.

**Warning signs in the gate itself**

- The team fixes one failure, reruns, and a new one appears. The gate is stopping at the first failure.
- The limits match the trial's numbers suspiciously well. They were probably written after the trial, not before.

**Quickest check**

Open the newest `grad-pack` run in MLflow. Compare each number to the criteria, and check that the criteria are dated before the trial started. Then compare `peak_tpm` to the capacity the app actually got.

learn:stops.a:
**Very little eval data.** A pass rate from a small eval set swings a lot. On 20 questions, one answer moves the score by 5 points, so a pass or fail near the limit may just be luck. Grow the eval set before you trust the number, and treat results close to the limit as "not sure yet."

**Real traffic differs from the trial.** The POC's `peak_tpm` (tokens a minute at the busiest time) comes from test users. Real users may ask longer questions or arrive all at once, and the questions themselves drift over time. Keep monitoring on rate-limit errors and cost, and re-run the gate on fresh numbers every few months.

**Stale evidence.** The gate reads the newest `grad-pack` run, but the team may have changed the prompt or model after logging it. Then the pack describes an app that no longer exists. Tag each pack with the app version, and have the gate reject packs older than the latest change.

learn:term.q: How is “proof of concept” different from “graduation pack”?
learn:term.a:
They are two different kinds of thing. The proof of concept is an **activity**. The graduation pack is a **record** of what that activity found.

The **proof of concept** (POC) is the small trial build. The team runs it in the shared experiment space to learn how well the app works, what it costs and how busy it gets.

The **graduation pack** is what the POC hands over. It holds six facts: a named owner, the pass rate, the must-pass result, the cost per success, the peak tokens a minute and the monitoring. In the stack, the POC logs these on one MLflow run named `grad-pack`.

Think of a school science experiment and its lab report. The experiment is where you test things. The report writes down the results. The teacher grades the report against a marking sheet written before you started.

In the lesson's example, the POC measured a pass rate of `0.86` and a cost per success of `0.12`. Those numbers go into the pack. The gate then reads the pack and compares it with the acceptance criteria. Those are the limits the team set before the POC began.

check:0:0.q: Why not “To save storage in the registry”?
check:0:0.a:
"To save storage in the registry" sounds sensible, but it does not match how a registry works.

The registry keeps every trained version anyway, whether you promote it or not. That is the point: you can always look back or roll back. Promoting a challenger does not add or delete anything. It just moves the `@champion` alias, which is a label pointing at a version number. Moving a label costs no extra storage. So the minimum gain has nothing to do with disk space.

What the option misses is the real risk: being fooled by chance. Scores on an evaluation set wobble a little from run to run. A challenger might score slightly higher just because of which examples happened to be in the data, not because it is truly better. If you promote on every tiny bump, you keep swapping models for no real benefit, and you might even swap in a worse one.

"A tiny gain is often just noise" is the right answer because the minimum gain makes sure a challenger wins by enough that the improvement is likely real, not luck.

check:0:2.q: Why not “MLflow refuses a smaller gain”?
check:0:2.a:
"MLflow refuses a smaller gain" sounds reasonable, but MLflow doesn't do that. The registry has no idea which version is "better." It stores versions and their metrics. An alias like `@champion` is just a pointer. `set_registered_model_alias` will move that pointer to any version you name, even a worse one.

What the option gets right: something does block small gains. But that something is **your** rule, written in your own code as `min_gain`. It's a team policy, not a tool limit.

It also misses the real question: **why** have the rule at all? Saying "the tool forces it" gives no reason. And if you think the tool protects you, you might skip writing the check yourself.

Here is the reason. Scores wobble. Run the same model on a slightly different set of examples, or have an LLM judge grade it twice, and the number shifts a little. A challenger that wins by a hair may not be better at all. It may just have had a lucky run.

"A tiny gain is often just noise" is better because it gives the actual reason: a small edge can come from random wobble rather than real improvement.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The noise explanation (scores shifting between runs or judge gradings) goes slightly beyond the lesson but does not contradict it, and the length is just under 200 words.

check:1:0.q: Why not “As the same judge: the prompt defines it”?
check:1:0.a:
That option gets one thing right. The prompt matters a lot. It holds the grading instructions, so it shapes how the judge thinks about a "good" answer.

What it misses is that a judge is two things: the prompt and the model that runs it. Swap the model and you have a different judge, even with the same words. A cheaper model might read the prompt more loosely or more strictly. It might miss details the old model caught. Any grade can shift.

Your champion judge earned `@champion` by agreeing often with grades people gave. That score belongs to the old prompt-and-model pair. It says nothing about the new pair. Keeping the old alias would trust a judge nobody has checked.

So save the new pair as its own version in the MLflow Prompt Registry, with the model recorded on it. Then let it compete. It earns `@challenger` by beating the champion judge by your minimum gain on the dev set. It takes `@champion` only after one check on the test set.

"As a new version that must earn its aliases" is better because changing the model changes the judge, so the new pair has to prove itself like any other challenger.

check:1:1.q: Why not “As a new version that keeps @champion”?
check:1:1.a:
That option gets one thing right. Swapping the model really does make a new judge. A judge is its grading prompt plus the model that runs it, so changing either half gives you a new pair. Saving it as a new version in the MLflow Prompt Registry, with the model recorded on it, is correct.

What it misses is the alias. `@champion` is a label that says "this is the judge we trust right now." Moving it to the new version straight away means you trust the cheaper model before testing it. A cheaper model may grade more harshly, more loosely, or less consistently. Every score it gives your model's champion and challenger could shift, and you would not know.

A new judge version is a challenger like any other. First it must agree with human grades more often than the current champion judge, by at least your minimum gain, on the dev set (the data you compare versions on). That earns it `@challenger`. Then it needs one check on the test set (data held back for a final confirmation) before it takes `@champion`.

"As a new version that must earn its aliases" is better because it records the change honestly and still makes the cheaper judge prove itself before anyone relies on its grades.

judge.notes: No significant problems; it is about 210 words, slightly over the target length, but still acceptable.

check:1:2.q: Why not “They split the traffic in half”?
check:1:2.a:
"They split the traffic in half" sounds reasonable, and it does touch on something real. Teams sometimes send part of the traffic to a new version to test it in the real world. That is called an A/B test, or a canary release when only a small slice goes to the newcomer. So the idea isn't silly.

But it's not what this rule says to do. The rule is a yes-or-no promotion check. You work out the threshold: the champion's 80 plus the agreed gain of 2, which makes 82. The challenger scores 81. That is better, but not better by enough. So it doesn't clear the bar, and nothing changes.

There's also a practical point. An alias like `@champion` points at exactly one version. It can't point at "half of version 3 and half of version 4." Splitting traffic would be a separate setup you choose on purpose. It doesn't happen automatically because a challenger came close.

"The champion stays" is better because 81 falls short of the 82 threshold, so the alias simply stays where it is.

check:2:0.a:
"Retrain version 5 overnight" has one good instinct. Version 5 is broken, and at some point you will want to find out why and build a better version.

But it misses the urgent part. Your users are getting bad answers right now. Retraining takes hours, so they keep getting bad answers all night. Retraining also might not fix the problem, since you don't yet know what went wrong. And whatever comes out is a brand-new version. It would have to start as a challenger and beat the champion on the same data before it could be promoted. So it is not a quick fix at all.

"Point `@champion` back to version 4" is better because version 4 is still sitting in the registry, already proven, and moving an alias (a name tag pointing at one version) takes seconds.

On Databricks, that rollback is one call:

```python
from mlflow import MlflowClient
MlflowClient(registry_uri="databricks-uc").set_registered_model_alias(
    "main.support.support_agent", "champion", version=4)
```

Anything loading `@champion` now gets version 4. Then you can investigate version 5 calmly.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Delete version 5 from the registry”?
check:2:2.a:
Deleting version 5 gets one thing right. You want version 5 to stop answering questions. That instinct is sound.

But it misses three things.

**It doesn't bring version 4 back.** The alias `@champion` is just a label pointing at one version. If you delete the version it points to, the label is left pointing at nothing. Anything that loads `@champion` now fails instead of getting good answers.

**It throws away evidence.** The registry keeps every version with its metrics so you can study it. If version 5 is gone, you can't dig into why it gave bad answers, or compare it with version 4.

**It can't be undone.** Deleting is permanent. Moving an alias is a small change you can make again at any time.

So deleting can come later, as cleanup, if you ever decide version 5 has no use.

The fix is one line that moves the label back:

```python
from mlflow import MlflowClient
MlflowClient(registry_uri="databricks-uc").set_registered_model_alias(
    "main.support.support_agent", "champion", version=4)
```

Pointing `@champion` back to version 4 is better because it restores the known-good model in seconds and keeps version 5 safe for investigation.

judge.notes: No real problems. Claims like deletion being permanent and the alias dangling go beyond the lesson but don't contradict it, and the length is borderline at about 200 words.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Keep the best so far” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem:* "We have a champion model serving live traffic and a few newer challengers. Swapping models for a tiny score bump adds risk without real benefit."

*The idea:* "First I set a bar: the champion's score plus a minimum gain. Then I walk through the challengers once and hold onto the best one so far, like keeping the tallest card you've seen. A challenger takes over only if it clears the bar and also beats the current best."

*The edge case:* "A tie is not a win, so the earlier version stays. If nobody clears the bar, the champion keeps the job."

**Likely follow-up:** "How do you know the scores are fair to compare?"

*Hint at a strong answer:* Say every version is scored on the same data by the same judge. The judge is a model that grades answers. It is versioned too, as one grading prompt plus the model that runs it. It has its own `@champion`, separate from your model's. (An alias is a movable name tag pointing at one version.) Then add that rollback is easy: you just move the `@champion` alias back to the old version.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **The champion keeps flipping.** `@champion` moves every few days on tiny gains. That usually means noise (random ups and downs) is being treated as real progress.
- **Scores were measured on different data.** One version was tested on easy examples and another on hard ones. The newer one looks better, then drops in real use.
- **Every score jumps at once.** Old and new versions all improve overnight. Often the judge changed, not the models. Someone edited the grading prompt or swapped its model without saving a new version.
- **Complaints rise after a promotion.** The dashboard looks fine, but real users notice worse answers.
- **Rollback is unclear.** Nobody knows which version `@champion` pointed to before, so moving it back is guesswork.

**Quickest check**

Pick the current champion and the version it replaced. Score both again on the same fixed dataset, using the same judge version. Here "judge version" means the prompt-and-model pair saved together. Is the gap still bigger than your `min_gain`? If not, the promotion was not earned. Move the alias back.

learn:stops.a:
**1. Your data changes over time.** Real questions drift, meaning they slowly stop looking like your old test data. A champion's old score may no longer reflect today. Refresh your evaluation set now and then, and score champion and challenger on that same refreshed set before comparing.

**2. You have very little data.** With only a few dozen examples, a small win can be pure luck. Raise your `min_gain`, collect more examples, or run the comparison several times before trusting a margin.

**3. Your app is an LLM scored by a judge.** Editing the judge's prompt or swapping its model can shift every grade. So treat a new judge as a challenger in its own right. It must beat the champion judge by your minimum gain on agreement with human grades on the dev set. Then it gets one check on the test set before it takes the judge's `@champion`. Until then, keep using the current champion judge. Always grade champion and challenger models with that same judge.

learn:term.a:
A **model registry** is a shared, organised store for trained models. It keeps every version you have saved, along with its scores (called **metrics**).

Think of a library's catalogue for one book series. Every edition sits on the shelf with a note about it. A sticky label saying "current edition" marks the one readers should borrow. If the new edition has a problem, you just move the label back to the old one. Nothing gets thrown away.

In the lesson, the sticky label is an **alias**, like `@champion`. It points at the version serving real traffic.

You can see the registry in the example's address:

```python
mlflow.pyfunc.load_model('models:/main.ml.churn@champion')
```

- `models:/` means "look in the model registry."
- `main.ml.churn` is the registered model's name. It works like the series title.
- `@champion` is the alias, so you get whichever version currently wears that label.

On Databricks, the registry lives in **Unity Catalog**, which is Databricks' central place for data and models. That's why the second example uses `registry_uri="databricks-uc"`. Moving `champion` to `version=4` is just moving the sticky label.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Yes: 2 out of 2 is a perfect score”?
check:0:0.a:
**What it gets right:** the math. 2 out of 2 really is 100%. Every trace the candidate handled passed.

**What it misses:** two traces is far too few to trust. A trace is one recorded run of your app answering one question. With only two, luck plays a huge part. Maybe those two questions were easy. One failure on the next question would drop the score to 2 out of 3, about 67%, which is worse than the 75% your current `production` version gets.

Compare that with the lesson's example. There, v3 had 100 traces at 90%. That many real questions makes a lucky streak much less likely.

This is also why you write the rule down first. The example rule says "at least 100 traces" before anything else. A perfect score on 2 traces never reaches that bar. So the decision is "keep testing," not "promote." Without that rule, a shiny 100% is tempting to act on.

**Why "Not yet: 2 traces is too few to tell" is better:** it sees that a score only counts once enough traces stand behind it.

judge.notes: Minor: it treats the example's 75% production rate as if it were the learner's own, though the Check question gives no production rate. Everything else is consistent with the lesson.

check:0:2.q: Why not “No: roll it back to the old prompt”?
check:0:2.a:
"No: roll it back" gets one thing right. It refuses to promote. With only 2 traces (2 recorded runs of the app answering a real question), promoting would be a guess, so saying "no" is sensible.

But rolling back is a different decision. It means you have evidence the candidate is *worse* and you want it gone. Here you have no such evidence. The candidate passed 2 out of 2. Nothing has failed. Pulling it now would throw away a version that might turn out to be better, based on no real signal.

The core problem is that 2 traces tell you almost nothing in either direction. One more failure would drop it to 67%. One more pass would keep it at 100%. The number swings wildly because the sample is tiny. That is why the lesson's rule sets a minimum, like at least 100 traces, before you compare pass rates at all.

Below that minimum, the honest move is to keep the canary running (keep sending a small share of real traffic to the candidate) and collect more traces.

"Not yet: 2 traces is too few to tell" is better because it names the real issue, too little data, and keeps testing instead of judging the prompt either way.

judge.notes: No real problems. It is about 200 words, right at the length limit, and could be trimmed slightly.

check:1:0.a:
"Keep testing" has a good instinct behind it. Being careful with real users is smart. And "keep" is a real outcome in this lesson. It's the right call when the new prompt hasn't had enough traces yet, or when its lead is too small to trust.

But neither of those is true here. Check the rule one piece at a time:

- **At least 100 traces?** The new prompt has 200. Yes.
- **At least 10 points better?** It beats the old one by 12. Yes.

Both conditions pass. (A "trace" is the saved record of one request, tagged with the prompt version it used.)

The reason you write the rule down *first* is so you don't second-guess it later. If you keep testing after the rule says go, you're quietly moving the goalposts. Meanwhile, most users stay on the weaker prompt for no clear reason.

"Promote it" is better because both written conditions are clearly met, and following your own rule is exactly what keeps the decision fair and repeatable.

check:1:1.a:
"Roll it back" gets one thing right. Rolling back is a real choice in this lesson. It means taking the new prompt out of use and sending everyone back to the old version. It's a sensible move, but only when the new version is doing worse.

That's not what happened here. Check the rule one part at a time:

- **At least 100 traces?** The new prompt has 200. A trace is the saved record of one real request, so there's enough evidence.
- **At least 10 points better?** It beats the old one by 12 points. It clears the bar.

Both conditions are met. Nothing in the numbers points toward a rollback. Picking it anyway would throw away a prompt that is clearly winning.

This is why you write the rule down first. Once the data comes in, you just follow it. You don't let a vague worry override it.

"Promote it" is better because the new prompt passes both parts of the written rule, so the rule says to give it the `production` alias.

judge.notes: Minor: the claim that rollback is 'only when the new version is doing worse' goes slightly beyond what the lesson states, but it is reasonable and does not contradict it.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Run an offline evaluation first”?
check:2:0.a:
"Run an offline evaluation first" is good advice. It just doesn't answer this question.

**What it gets right:** Offline evaluation is a real step in the lesson. You score a new prompt on your eval set (your saved test questions) with `mlflow.genai.evaluate` before any user sees it. That's a smart habit.

**What it misses:** The question asks what you *can't* do once traces are mixed with no version tag. Offline evaluation doesn't use those live traces at all. It runs on your saved questions. So missing tags don't block it. You could still run it today.

What the missing tags break is the canary step. The canary sends a small share of real traffic to the new version. Without a `prompt_version` tag, you can't tell which traces came from v2 and which came from v3. You can't count passes per version, so you can't apply your promote, keep-testing, or roll-back rule.

"Compare the versions on real questions" is better because that comparison depends on the version tag, so it's the thing you actually lose.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Give the new one a canary share”?
check:2:1.a:
Good question. It's a tempting pick, because canaries are a real part of this lesson.

A **canary** means sending a small share of real users to the new version first, like 10 in 100. That's a smart way to roll out safely. But look at where the split happens: in your own code, when it picks `cand` or `prod`. The version tag isn't needed for that. So even with untagged traces, you can still give the new version a canary share.

What the missing tag breaks is the step *after* the canary. A **trace** is the saved record of one request: the question, the answer, and the steps in between. If traces carry no `prompt_version` tag, they're one big pile. You can't filter with `search_traces` to pull out just version 3. So you can't count passes per version. Then your written rule, like "at least 100 traces and 10 points better," has nothing to check.

"Compare the versions on real questions" is better because that's the exact thing the tag makes possible, and losing the tag means losing it.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Count passes per version, then compare” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

*The problem:* "We changed a prompt, a saved set of instructions for the model, and needed to know if the new version was really better on live questions, not just on our test set."

*The idea:* "We tagged every trace, the saved record of one request, with its prompt version. That let us count passes for each version separately. Then we turned the counts into pass rates and applied a rule we wrote down before looking: promote, keep testing, or roll back."

*Trade-off:* "The canary, the new version, gets less traffic, so its numbers are shaky early on. Comparing raw counts is unfair too. 300 passes beats 90, but 90 of 100 is 90% and 300 of 400 is only 75%. So we compare rates, and we wait for enough traces before trusting them."

**A likely follow-up**

*"Why write the rule down before you see the results?"*

Hint for a strong answer: if you pick the rule afterwards, you can talk yourself into whatever you hoped to see. A rule fixed in advance keeps the decision honest and repeatable.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
Here are the signs that the rollout was skipped or done wrong.

**Traces with no version tag.** Some traces have no `prompt_version` tag. Then you can't tell which prompt gave which answer, so any comparison is a guess.

**Counts that don't add up.** The candidate should get about 10 in 100 users. If it gets almost none, or almost all, the traffic split is broken.

**A big win on a tiny sample.** For example, "5 of 5 passed, 100%!" Five traces prove very little. Your rule's minimum trace count exists to stop this.

**A rule that moved.** The threshold changed after someone saw the results. That means the decision was made first and the rule was bent to fit it.

**Offline looked great, real use drops.** The candidate scored high on your eval set (your saved test questions). On real questions, its pass rate falls. Your eval set may not look like real traffic.

**Quickest check:** search your traces by the `prompt_version` tag. Count traces and passes for each version, and compare those totals to all traces. Check three things:

- Untagged traces should be zero.
- The candidate's share should be near 10%.
- Each version needs enough traces to meet your rule.

judge.notes: Minor: the answer is right at the ~200-word limit, and the "candidate's share near 10%" check is a rough proxy because the split is by user, not by trace.

learn:stops.a:
**1. Very little traffic.** If only a few hundred people use your app each week, reaching 100 candidate traces can take a long time. Small counts also swing a lot by luck, so a 90% on 100 traces might shrink later. Lean harder on the offline eval, wait longer, or ask for a bigger gap before you promote.

**2. Traffic that changes over time, or uneven users.** Splitting by `user_id` is fair only if both groups ask similar questions. If the candidate group happens to hold your heaviest users, or a product launch shifts what people ask, the comparison gets skewed. Compare both versions over the same time window, and check pass rates per question type, not just overall.

**3. A bigger system with many moving parts.** In a RAG app (one that looks up documents before answering), the model, the retriever, or the document index can change during your test. Then a better score might not come from the prompt at all. Tag traces with those versions too, and change one thing at a time.

learn:term.a:
**Offline evaluation** means testing a new prompt on your own saved questions before any real user sees it. "Offline" just means "not live." No customer is involved yet.

Think of a chef trying a new recipe. Before it goes on the menu, they cook it in the back kitchen and taste it themselves. Only if it tastes right does it reach a few diners.

In this lesson, that back-kitchen step comes first. You take your **eval set**, which is your saved test questions. You run the candidate prompt on them with `mlflow.genai.evaluate`. That function scores each answer, so you can see how the new version does.

If it looks good, you move to the **canary** step. A canary is a small share of real traffic, here 10 in 100 users, sent to the new version. The lesson's numbers (v2 at 75%, v3 at 90%) come from that live step, not from the offline one.

So offline evaluation is the safety check that happens before the canary even starts.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Wait a week to collect more data first”?
check:0:0.a:
"Wait a week to collect more data first" gets one thing right. One hour is not much data, and a single bad hour can be a fluke. More data does make a comparison more trustworthy.

But it misses why the canary exists. A canary is there to catch problems while only a few users can see them. The **error rate** is the share of requests that fail. If it has doubled, real people are hitting failures right now. Waiting a week means 10% of users keep getting a worse agent for seven more days. That is the exact harm the canary was meant to limit.

You also don't need to wait to learn more. The failed requests already left **traces**. A trace is a step-by-step record of what the agent did on one request. Those records can show you why it failed.

Rolling back is cheap too. Setting `support_agent-4` to 0% sends everyone back to `support_agent-3`. You can fix the problem and try the canary again later.

"Move its traffic back to 0% and look at its traces" is better because it stops the harm right away and still lets you find the cause from data you already have.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Switch everyone to it to get more data”?
check:0:2.a:
"Switch everyone to it to get more data" gets one thing right. More traffic does give you more examples to study. But it misses the whole point of a canary.

A canary exists to limit harm. Only 10% of users see the new version, so if it breaks, most people are safe. A doubled error rate is already a clear warning. Switching everyone over would turn a small problem into a big one. Every user would now hit those errors.

You also don't need more traffic to learn what went wrong. The first hour has already produced plenty of **traces**, the step-by-step records of what the agent did on each request. Those failed requests are your evidence.

Rolling back is cheap. You set the new version's share to 0% and the old one back to 100%:

```python
{"served_entity_name": "support_agent-3", "traffic_percentage": 100},
{"served_entity_name": "support_agent-4", "traffic_percentage": 0},
```

"Move its traffic back to 0% and look at its traces" is better because it protects users right away while still letting you study the failures you already collected.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The 10% share and the claim of 'plenty' of traces are mild assumptions, but they are consistent with the lesson's example.

check:1:0.q: Why not “All of it, it passed the tests”?
check:1:0.a:
**"All of it, it passed the tests"** gets one thing right: tests matter. You shouldn't ship version 4 if it fails them.

But tests only cover the cases someone thought to write. Real users ask odd questions, word things strangely, and hit situations nobody planned for. An agent can pass every test and still give weaker answers, call tools wrongly, or run slower or costlier with real traffic.

If version 4 gets all the traffic and has a hidden problem, every user hits it at once. You learn about it from complaints, not from your own checks.

A canary release limits that risk. Only a few users see the new version. You compare its traces against version 3's. Traces are the step-by-step record of what the agent did. You also compare evals, which are scored checks of answer quality. If version 4 looks good, you raise its share. If not, you set it to 0% and everyone is back on version 3.

**"A small share, like 10 in 100"** is better because real traffic gets to test version 4, while any problem reaches only a few users and is easy to undo.

check:1:2.a:
"None until next month" gets one thing right. It is careful. If version 4 has a bug, nobody sees it, because nobody uses it.

But waiting teaches you very little. Your tests before launch use examples you picked yourself. Real users ask stranger questions. You only see how version 4 behaves when real requests reach it.

So after a month of waiting, you still don't know if version 4 is good. And on the day you finally switch, you face the risky choice the lesson warns about: moving everyone at once. Meanwhile, any fixes in version 4 sit unused for a month.

A canary gives you real evidence without much risk. You compare its traces (the step-by-step records of what the agent did) and evals (scored checks of its answers) against version 3. If something looks wrong, you roll back by setting version 4 to 0%.

**"A small share, like 10 in 100" is better because you learn from real traffic right away, while only a few users are exposed if something goes wrong.**

check:2:1.q: Why not “Switch everyone over at once”?
check:2:1.a:
"Switch everyone over at once" gets one thing right. The canary looks healthy, so moving forward is the correct direction. Staying at 10% forever would waste a good version.

What it misses is how little a day at 10% really tells you. Some problems only show up with more users. That includes rare questions, odd edge cases, and the strain of heavier load. Your traces (the step-by-step records of what the agent did) and evals (the scored test checks) only cover the traffic the canary actually saw.

If you jump straight to 100% and one of those hidden problems appears, every user hits it at once. You can still roll back, but the damage is already wide.

Moving bit by bit keeps each step small. You might go to 25%, then 50%, then 100%. At each stop you check traces and evals again. The next step might look like this:

```python
{"served_entity_name": "support_agent-3", "traffic_percentage": 50},
{"served_entity_name": "support_agent-4", "traffic_percentage": 50},
```

"Move more traffic to it, bit by bit" is better because it keeps gathering evidence while keeping any surprise small and easy to undo.

judge.notes: Minor: the 'next step' snippet shows 50/50 right after saying the path starts at 25%, but this does not contradict the lesson.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Set it to 0% to be safe”?
check:2:2.a:
Setting the canary to 0% gets one thing right. It is the lesson's rollback move. If the new version (the canary) misbehaves, dropping it to 0% sends everyone back to the old version, quickly and safely.

But rollback is for when something is wrong. Here, nothing is wrong. The canary ran for a day, and its traces (records of what the agent did on each request) and evals (scored tests of its answers) look as good as the old version's. That is the evidence you were waiting for.

Pulling it to 0% now throws that evidence away. The new version never ships, and you learn nothing more. "Safe" here just means "stuck." You can always roll back later if a problem shows up, because 0% is only one setting away.

The better answer is "Move more traffic to it, bit by bit." It acts on the good results while still limiting risk, since each small step lets you check the traces and evals again before going further.

For example, the next split might be:

```python
routes = [
  {"served_entity_name": "support_agent-3", "traffic_percentage": 75},
  {"served_entity_name": "support_agent-4", "traffic_percentage": 25},
]
```

judge.notes: No clear problems. The answer is near the 200-word limit, and the 'better answer' part runs slightly past one sentence, but it still fits.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Add up percents until you pass” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem:* "In a canary release, I send a small share of traffic, say 10%, to the new agent version. I also want each user to always get the same version, so their experience doesn't flip between requests."

*The idea:* "I turn the user's id into a bucket from 0 to 99 with `user_id % 100`. That is the remainder after dividing by 100. Then I walk through the routes once, adding each percent to a running total. The first route whose total is bigger than the bucket answers. With a 90/10 split, buckets 0 to 89 go to `support_agent-3`, and buckets 90 to 99 go to `support_agent-4`."

*Edge case:* "The percents should add up to 100. If they add up to less, some buckets match no route. So I'd check the total up front or have a fallback."

**A likely follow-up**

"What happens to users when you raise the canary from 10% to 25%?"

*Hint for a strong answer:* The new version now gets buckets 75 to 99. Users in buckets 90 to 99 stay on the new version. Users in buckets 75 to 89 move over to it. Nobody already on the canary gets sent back to the old version.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The 10%→25% follow-up assumes the routes stay in the same order, and the answer runs right at the 200-word limit.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **Everyone breaks at once.** If complaints or error rates jump for all users the moment you deploy, the new version probably got 100% of traffic. A real canary only hurts the small slice.
- **The split doesn't match the plan.** You set 90/10, but your logs show something like 50/50, or 100/0. Check that the route names exactly match your served versions, such as `support_agent-4`.
- **One user gets flip-flopping answers.** The same person sees different tone or behaviour from one message to the next. That means requests are not pinned to their user id, so they bounce between versions.
- **You can't tell the versions apart.** If your traces (the step-by-step records of each request) don't say which version answered, you can't compare them. The canary then teaches you nothing.
- **The canary looks too good.** A tiny sample can hide problems. Wait for enough requests before you increase the share.

**Quickest check**

Pull an hour of traces. Count how many each version answered and compare against 90/10. Then pick one user id and confirm every one of their requests went to the same version.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three places where a simple percentage canary needs extra care.

**Very little traffic.** If your agent gets only a few dozen requests a day, 10% gives you a handful of traces. That is too few to tell a real difference from luck. Run offline evals on a saved test set first, then keep the canary running longer before you judge it.

**User ids that aren't evenly spread.** Taking `user_id % 100` assumes the last two digits are spread out fairly. Some id schemes break that, and anonymous users may have no id at all. Run the id through a hash first. A hash is a function that scrambles any value into an evenly spread number. For users without an id, use a session id instead.

**Agents that take real actions.** Some agents send emails, update tickets, or remember past chats. Setting the canary to 0% stops new traffic, but it does not undo what the new version already did. Test risky tools in a dry-run mode first. A dry run means the tool reports what it would do without doing it. Also keep one whole conversation on the same version.

learn:term.a:
A **canary release** means trying a new version on a few people before giving it to everyone.

Think of a restaurant changing its soup recipe. The chef doesn't swap it for every table on day one. She serves the new soup to one table in ten and watches their faces. If they like it, more tables get it. If not, she quietly goes back to the old recipe.

The name comes from coal miners. They carried a canary bird underground. If the air turned bad, the bird showed it first, so the miners could get out in time. The new version plays the bird's role. It warns you early, while only a few users are affected.

In the lesson's example, two versions of the agent run on the same Databricks **serving endpoint** (the web address your app sends requests to):

- `support_agent-3` is the old, trusted version. It gets 90% of traffic.
- `support_agent-4` is the canary. It gets 10%.

You compare their traces (records of what each agent did) and evals (quality scores). If version 4 looks good, you raise its share. If it misbehaves, you set it to 0%. That is your rollback.
